title: Job loses everything (Job 1–2)
hook: a good man loses children, wealth and health; his friends first sit silent seven days

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah sat east of Nineveh, angry at mercy, and God asked a question. Your line was should I not spare them.

The book opens like a folk tale, in the Douay-Rheims: "There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job." Simple and upright, fearing God. Seven sons, three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, the greatest man in the East. Then the scene shifts to heaven, where the sons of God come before the Lord, and among them is Satan; the Hebrew says ha-satan, the adversary, with the article, like a title in the court. God points out Job. The adversary shrugs: does Job fear God for nothing? Take it all away and see.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF HUS.` → `THE ADVERSARY IN THE COURT.` → `DOES JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOTHING?`

segments.voice: Then the messengers start arriving, each still speaking when the next runs in. Raiders took the oxen. Fire fell and burned the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And the last: a great wind struck the house where your children were eating, and it fell on them, and they are dead. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and worships: naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked I shall return. The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. Then his health goes too, sores from his feet to his head, and he sits on a dunghill scraping himself with a broken piece of pottery. Three friends hear of it, Eliphaz, Baldad and Sophar, and agree to come together to comfort him. From far off they don't recognize him. They weep aloud, tear their robes, throw dust over their heads. And then the Douay says: "they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no man spoke to him a word: for they saw that his grief was very great." Seven days. No speeches. Nobody explained anything. In chapter three Job finally speaks, and then the friends start answering, and for chapter after chapter they explain his suffering to him: he must have done something. At the very end, God says they did not speak rightly about him. So the part Job's friends got right was the first week, on the ground, with their mouths shut.
screen: `MESSENGER AFTER MESSENGER.` · `THE LORD GAVE, THE LORD HATH TAKEN.` · `SEVEN DAYS ON THE GROUND, NO WORD.` · `THEN THEY STARTED EXPLAINING.` · then, large: `THEY SAW THAT HIS GRIEF WAS VERY GREAT.`

segments.voice: If someone comes to mind whose grief is very great, picture arriving and sitting down on the ground beside them. Notice the urge to say something, a reason, a bright side, a story about your own aunt, and let it pass, and stay. If you pray, hold that person before God without words.
ha-satan. Hebrew for the adversary: the heavenly accuser who challenged God to strip Job of his children, his wealth and his health. Today's word.
Your line: they sat with him. Seven days, and not one word. Day four hundred thirty-one, done.

howItsDone: The Church's traditional Office of the Dead draws its readings from Job, and at Catholic wakes visitors come to keep company with the grieving family as much as to speak.

fork.setup: you're Eliphaz. you've traveled to comfort your friend, and you find him unrecognizable, sitting on a dunghill scraping his sores. what do you do?
options: explain that God must be punishing something he did.
sit down on the ground with him and say nothing.
pray aloud over him and leave.
fork.reveal: seven days and seven nights, and no man spoke to him a word. the trouble begins later, when they start explaining.

original.note: Hebrew: the adversary, with the definite article, a role in the heavenly court in Job 1–2.

trapdoor: what you thought: the patience of Job, a man who never complained.
what it means: a good man loses everything, and his friends' best comfort is a week of silence; when they start explaining, they go wrong.
what a scholar hears: ha-satan with the article, a courtroom role; the prose frame of chapters 1–2 and 42 wraps long poems of argument.
guess: the adversary, an accuser in God's court
one of Job's three friends who came to comfort
the messenger who brought Job bad news

chat.says: My friend just lost her dad. What do Job's friends teach about helping?
options: Their best part came first: seven days sitting beside him, saying nothing at all.
Give her a long talk about why suffering happens, so she can make sense of it.
Remind her quickly of the bright side, so the grief doesn't last long.
chat.meaning: The friends sat with Job seven days without a word, for his grief was very great. Their explanations came later, and God said they didn't speak rightly.

ha-satan.meaning: Hebrew: the adversary, like a title in the heavenly court

Hus.meaning: the land where Job lived, in the Douay

Eliphaz.meaning: one of three friends who came to comfort Job

Baldad.meaning: another of the friends who sat silent with Job

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the hook now names Satan as the Douay does before giving the Hebrew ha-satan; replaced a myth that told Catholics their reading of 'Satan' was wrong with one from the text (Job worships, does not curse); cut the uncited 'for centuries' Office of the Dead claim from the teach and softened it in howItsDone; 'most of the book' and 'the best thing' softened.
Douay-Rheims wording of Job 1:1 and 2:13 quoted from memory; please check.
Job 1:21 ('the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away') is given in paraphrase, unquoted, since the Douay's full verse runs differently from the familiar form.
Friends' names in the Douay: Eliphaz the Themanite, Baldad the Suhite, Sophar the Naamathite. Confirm.
Readings from Job in the traditional Office of the Dead (Matins lessons): confirm the phrase 'for centuries'.
The 'patience of Job' (James 5:11) is mentioned only in the trapdoor's first floor as a common impression.
